headline: Any n points in d ≥ 3 dimensions span at least a constant times n^(2/d) distinct distances, the paper claims.
scope: The result covers every finite set of distinct points in d-dimensional space, for each fixed d of at least 3. It makes no assumption on where the points sit.
plain: Place n points in space and list all the distances between pairs. Erdős asked how few different distances there can be. In d dimensions a grid gives about n^(2/d), and the conjecture says nothing does better by more than a constant factor. This paper claims to prove that for every fixed d of at least 3. No Lean formalization is listed.
doesNot: This does not touch the flat, two-dimensional case, which has a different conjectured answer, and it gives no numerical value for the constant.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Paul Erdős, who posed the distinct-distances problem
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles the higher-dimensional form of a famous problem with the best possible power.

visual.title: Best proven exponent for distinct distances among n points in four dimensions
visual.note: Higher is better. The conjectured exponent is 2/4 = 0.5. The 2026 bound of about 0.471 also loses an o(1) in the exponent.

explanation:
Build a cube-shaped grid of points, 10 on a side, so 1,000 points in all. Measure the distance between every pair. Squared distances are whole numbers from 1 up to 3 × 9², which is 243. A direct count finds only 144 different distances among almost half a million pairs. For comparison, 1,000 raised to the power 2/3 is 100.

That is the pattern behind the question. In d dimensions, a grid with n points spans about n^(2/d) distances, up to a constant factor[4]. Erdős introduced the distinct-distances problem in 1946[1]. The higher-dimensional conjecture says no set of n points can do better than a constant times n^(2/d)[2].

The paper claims exactly that bound[3]. For each d of at least 3, there is a constant c_d above zero. Every set of n ≥ 2 points spans at least c_d × n^(2/d) distances[3]. No assumption is made on where the points sit[5]. The constant depends only on the dimension, and the paper gives no number for it.

Earlier bounds fell short in the power. In three dimensions, Aronov, Pach, Sharir and Tardos reached about n^(77/141), roughly n^0.546[6]. Solymosi and Vu built recurrences linking dimensions[7]. Their original theorem gives about n^0.5643 in three dimensions[8]. In four dimensions it gives n^(5/12), about n^0.417[8]. In 2026, Tidor, Yu and Zakharov proved n^(2/3 − o(1)) in three dimensions[9]. Fed into the recurrences, that gives n^(8/17 − o(1)) in four dimensions[10]. That is about n^0.471, still short of 0.5[11].

An earlier manuscript by Aksoy Yazici claimed the same constant-factor bound. Its author withdrew it, because the proof of its Theorem 1.2 is not correct[12].

Why does the constant factor matter in three dimensions, where the power 2/3 was nearly reached? A bound like n^(2/3 − o(1)) still allows the ratio to the target to shrink forever, just very slowly[13]. Ruling that out means excluding every slowly shrinking ratio, without first fixing a power saving[14].

The single hard part is concentration. Bounds from lower dimensions limit how many points can sit on one flat plane or line[15]. They do not stop points from crowding onto curved surfaces, and no single polynomial degree captures all such crowding[15]. The paper handles this by tracking crowding at many polynomial degree scales at once[16]. Its main step rules out a covering by thin cones [shapes swept out by lines through one point][17].

The flat, two-dimensional case is different. There a square grid gives about n divided by the square root of log n distances, so the conjectured answer has another form[18]. Guth and Katz proved a bound of n divided by log n in the plane in 2015. This paper uses that planar result as its starting input[19].

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. The constant c_d is not given as a number, and an earlier claim of the same bound was withdrawn. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: The number of different values among all distances between pairs of points in a set.
A fixed multiplier that does not grow or shrink with the number of points.
A small loss in the power that shrinks to zero as n grows, but may shrink very slowly.
An inequality that turns a bound in one dimension into a bound in a higher dimension.
The highest power allowed in the polynomial equations used to describe where points crowd.
A shape made of straight lines all passing through one point.
